messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Loss of Control: Lack of control
  Maladaptive Strategies: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Hopelessness: I have no future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Malik was 21, an African American chef working long shifts in a busy restaurant kitchen, when he first came to treatment saying that what happened to him had changed the way he moved through ordinary life. The assault had taken place after work, when he had been in a situation where he felt he had little control over what was happening around him. He described the event only in fragments at first, but the central fact was clear: he had been sexually assaulted by others, and the experience left him with a lasting sense of violation and helplessness. In the months that followed, Malik found that violence of any kind could set him on edge, and even sounds of cars passing or pulling up outside could jolt him into a state of immediate alarm. He noticed this most acutely in his neighborhood and around the restaurant, where delivery cars and engines in the alley were part of the normal rhythm of the day. A sudden rev of a motor or the sharp approach of a vehicle would make his whole body tighten before he had time to think, as if something dangerous was about to happen again.

At work, Malik kept himself busy and tried to stay focused on prep tasks, but he also began checking his body constantly for signs that something was wrong, running his hands over his arms, chest, and sides as though he might find proof of injury or danger there. He described this as a habit he did almost without noticing, especially when he was moving between stations in the kitchen. If a coworker came up behind him too quickly, or made a sudden movement with a pan or tray, he would become immediately guarded, watching their hands and stepping back before he could fully register what was happening. Even at home, where he lived alone, he no longer felt settled. He said he felt on guard inside his own apartment, listening to sounds from the hall or outside the window, unable to fully let his shoulders drop.

The memories came back in a way that felt intrusive and disorganizing. Malik said that something in the environment could bring back the full memory without warning, and that when it happened he was suddenly back in the event before he understood how he had got there. He could be at work hearing a car door slam outside, or at home hearing a vehicle pass slowly on the street, and then the scene would come back with such force that it felt immediate rather than remembered. In those moments, he also noticed that certain sounds seemed to return in his head exactly as they had been during the assault, as if the original noises were playing again inside him. When he tried to talk about what happened, he often lost the thread and could not finish. He would start explaining, then stop, stare downward, and say he could not put the pieces together in a way that made sense. He found this frustrating and shameful, particularly because he was used to being capable and in control in his work.

Malik had also come to think differently about himself and about what the assault meant. He said he imagined getting revenge on the people responsible, and these thoughts appeared in response to the sense that what had happened to him was wrong and left unanswered. At the same time, he was haunted by the belief that he had acted in ways that went against who he was. He did not describe those actions in detail, but he spoke with clear self-reproach, as if the event had forced him to see himself as someone who had not lived up to his own values. He also believed that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, and he returned to that thought repeatedly, comparing himself to an imagined person who would have done things differently. That comparison fed into a deep hopelessness. He said plainly that he had no future, and this was not dramatic in his telling but flat and resigned, as though he could no longer picture life opening back up.

Over time, Malik’s day-to-day life narrowed. He kept working because the restaurant gave him structure, but he found himself distracted by the need to scan for danger and by the strain of trying not to be caught off guard by sounds or sudden movements. The kitchen, with its clatter of pans, shouted orders, and cars pulling up for deliveries, gave him repeated contact with the very cues that set off his alarm. He had begun to avoid talking about the assault with anyone because each attempt left him feeling more fragmented, and he was increasingly isolated with his own thoughts. What finally brought him in was the sense that he could not keep living in a state where ordinary moments at home or at work could turn into full alarm without warning. He came hoping for relief from the constant sense that danger was close, and he was most afraid that the future he could not imagine for himself was in fact already gone.
